title: Cisco Secure Endpoint Retrospective Detections
exclusions: Covers files the connector saw on disk. Files that never touched a host with a connector are not included; look for the same hash in email and proxy logs to see how it arrived.
evidence: Saved alert results per hash with the host list, and the ticket showing each host was checked and cleaned.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Pick a Retrospective Detection from the Secure Endpoint console Events page in the last 90 days and run the search over the same window. It returns a row for that file hash, and `hosts` matches the computers the console lists for it.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run the search over a window in which the console shows no Retrospective Detection events. It returns no rows, while other `cisco:se` event types for the same window are still present.

dataSources: `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Secure Endpoint input, which polls `GET /v1/events`. This search uses event type 553648147 (Retrospective Detection). Each event carries `event_type`, `event_type_id`, `detection`, `severity`, `connector_guid`, `group_guids{}`, `computer.hostname`, `computer.user`, `computer.external_ip`, `computer.links.trajectory`, and for file events `file.file_name`, `file.file_path`, `file.disposition`, and `file.identity.sha256`.
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Cisco Secure Endpoint input.
spl:
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id=553648147
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| eval disposition='file.disposition'
| stats dc(host_name) as host_count values(host_name) as hosts values(file_name) as files values(file_path) as paths values(detection) as detections min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by sha256
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - host_count
description: Groups Secure Endpoint retrospective detections by file hash. A retrospective detection means a file the connector saw earlier, while it was still considered clean or unknown, has now been judged malicious. Each row shows how many hosts have the file, their names, the file names and paths, and the detection names.
value: Retrospective detection is how malware that was new when it arrived still gets found. The hash view shows the full spread of one file across the estate in one row, so responders clean every host that ran it instead of only the first one to alert.
implementation: Collect Secure Endpoint events with the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) input into `index=secure_endpoint`. Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and alert on every row.
visualization: Alert table: sha256, host_count, hosts, files, paths, detections, firstTime, lastTime. Supporting panel: retrospective detections per week over 90 days (column chart).

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Verdict reversals** — Cisco occasionally reclassifies a file and later reverses it; the console shows a Retrospective Restore event when that happens. Check for one before reimaging.

2. **Archived copies** — files in backup folders or mail stores are detected but were never run. Use the trajectory to see whether the file executed.

**Suppression:** throttle per hash for 24 hours.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs.
• A Secure Endpoint API credential: in the Secure Endpoint console under Administration > API Credentials, create a read-only credential and record the client ID and API key, plus the API host for your region (for example `api.amp.cisco.com` for North America, `api.eu.amp.cisco.com` for Europe).
• Outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the input host to the API host.
• An index for Secure Endpoint data (this page uses `index=secure_endpoint`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the SOC and endpoint teams.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Cisco Secure Endpoint card, and create an input with the API host, client ID, and API key. Set the index to `secure_endpoint`. The modular input polls `GET /v1/events` with a default interval of 300 seconds and writes `sourcetype=cisco:se`.
• Select the event types the input should collect. Collecting all types is simplest; if you limit them, include the event type IDs this search uses.
• In a distributed deployment run the input on one node only; the guide notes that the computers, compromises, and top-malware endpoints can produce duplicates otherwise.
• Check the events this search needs: run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se event_type_id=553648147 | stats count by detection` over 90 days.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id=553648147
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| eval disposition='file.disposition'
| stats dc(host_name) as host_count values(host_name) as hosts values(file_name) as files values(file_path) as paths values(detection) as detections min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by sha256
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - host_count
```

Understanding this SPL
• 553648147 is Retrospective Detection; Secure Endpoint raises it on every host that has the file once the verdict changes to malicious.
• `stats ... by sha256` turns many host events into one row per file, with `dc(host_name)` as the spread.
• The search does not rely on `disposition` because it is the current verdict, which is malicious for every event of this type.

Step 3 — Validate
• Compare with the Secure Endpoint console Events page filtered to Retrospective Detection for the same time range: the hosts per hash should match.
• Search the hash in the console's File Trajectory and confirm the same host list.
• Run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se | timechart span=1h count by event_type` over 7 days; flat zero for all types for more than two intervals means the input stopped, not that the estate is clean.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and throttle on `sha256` for 24 hours.
• Route to the SOC with the host list. For each host, check the device trajectory to see whether the file ran, and isolate the host if it did.
• Search the hash in email and proxy logs to find the delivery path.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No cisco:se events and HTTP 401 in the input log: wrong client ID or API key, or the API host is for a different region from the organisation.
• Events arrive but `event_type_id` is missing: the events were indexed before JSON extraction applied; check `| fieldsummary` on one hour of data.
• Duplicate events with the same `id`: the input runs on more than one node, or the legacy AMP for Endpoints input (Splunkbase 3686) is still enabled. Keep one collector.
grandmaExplanation: Sometimes a file only turns out to be bad days after it arrived. When that happens, we list every computer that has it, so all of them get cleaned.
